query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The premelting and melting behavior of solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by kinetically restricted, stochastic nucleation of local liquid regions. Limited atomic mobility in the solid precursor leads to nanoscale compositional fluctuations and lattice strains that lower the local melting points. These local inhomogeneities then promote a gradual and heterogeneous melting process, in contrast to the abrupt melting observed in simpler binary alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu with homogeneous average composition but with inherent nanoscale compositional fluctuations and strain.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating across the premelting to melting temperature range under an inert atmosphere, monitored using in-situ high-resolution imaging techniques.
generation.conditions: Heating experiments performed at controlled rates (both fast and slow) in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with particle sizes in the nanometer regime where diffusion is limited.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale compositional fluctuations and lattice strain within each nanoparticle that create locally reduced melting thresholds.
generation.mechanism: Due to limited atomic mobility in the solid phase (stemming from high configurational entropy and kinetic constraints inherited from the synthesis), some regions within the nanoparticle undergo local premelting at temperatures below the bulk melting point. As temperature increases, these isolated liquid domains coalesce, resulting in an overall heterogeneous melting behavior that is influenced by the stochastic distribution of local compositions and defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: During heating, in-situ observations will reveal the appearance of localized 'liquid spots' or regions of reduced crystallinity at sub-melting temperatures, eventually merging into a fully molten state. Compared to simpler (e.g., binary) alloy nanoparticles, the high-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit a more gradual onset of melting and a broader temperature interval over which melting occurs.
generation.baseline: Binary or simpler multi-component alloy nanoparticles that have higher atomic mobility and more uniform melting behavior, characterized by a relatively sharp melting point.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles synthesized under conditions of limited free-atom mobility (e.g., solid precursor reduction or rapid high-temperature processing) and may not extend to systems synthesized by methods that allow extensive atomic rearrangement or in liquid-phase processes where diffusion is less restricted.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range over which local premelting initiates and the statistical variation of these local melting sites remain to be quantitatively determined. The influence of specific preparation methods and particle size distributions on this behavior also requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) heating of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles at various controlled heating rates under an inert atmosphere. Monitor the onset and spatial distribution of local melting using diffraction pattern changes and imaging. A controlled comparison should be made with similarly sized binary alloy nanoparticles. Additionally, apply fast scanning calorimetry to detect the temperature spread of the melting transition.
measurements: Spatially-resolved TEM images to detect localized liquid regions or loss of crystallinity.
In-situ electron diffraction to monitor gradual loss of lattice order.
Calorimetric measurements tracking the broadness of the melting peak.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles exhibit a uniform and sharp melting transition at a temperature close to the bulk melting point, with no observable evidence of locally initiated melting or heterogeneous premelting regions regardless of heating rate, then the hypothesis that limited atomic mobility and nanoscale fluctuations drive a stochastic premelting process would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. By analyzing the TEM images and EDS elemental mappings (Fig. 1h), all five elements relatively homogeneously are distributed within the CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles, in which the contents of the Fe, Co and Ni elements are higher than those of the Cr and Mn (Fig. S3), benefiting from their closer reduction potential and fewer valence electrons that form stable compounds while Mn is expected to be partially vaporized during the laser synthesis due to its higher vapor pressure. Moreover, the boiling temperature of 2334 K (Table S3) of Mn is the lowest and close to the highest temperature induced by laser, thus the Mn element has a relatively high possibility to evaporate. The HRTEM images in Fig. 1f and Fig. S4b–d, also show that the HEA nanoparticles are partially embraced by several graphene layers. AbstractThe single-step incorporation of multiple immiscible elements into colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles has manifold technological potential, but it continues to be a challenge for state-of-the-art synthesis methods. Hence, the development of a synthesis approach by which the chemical composition and phase of colloidal HEA nanoparticles can be controlled could lead to a new pool of nanoalloys with unparalleled functionalities. Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals. Further, the scalability of the process with an unprecedented productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour is demonstrated. Electrochemical analysis reveals a unique redox behavior of the particles' surfaces in an alkaline environment and a potential for future application as a heterogeneous catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction.
